title: yamt
tagline: A three-way merge window like the one in JetBrains IDEs, for every git conflict at once. 🔀
why: JetBrains IDE's three-pane merge window is the only merge tool I find usable. VS Code's merge editor, its extensions and the TUI mergetools all felt unintuitive.

They all start from the `<<<<<<<` conflict markers. Once git has collapsed a merge into markers the base is gone, so you can see _that_ two sides differ but not _what each side changed_. yamt never parses a conflict marker: it reads the base, your side and theirs from git's index and diffs them itself.

`git mergetool` opens one file at a time, and real merges touch many files. yamt takes over the whole merge: every conflicted file in one window, your side on the left, theirs on the right, the result in the middle.

sections.title: Install
body: - **Linux**: the `.AppImage` or the `.deb`. The `.deb` (`sudo apt install ./yamt_0.6.4_amd64.deb`)
puts `yamt` on your PATH. For the AppImage, put it there yourself.
With AppImageLauncher (it stops a copy outside its folder with a dialog): let it integrate the
AppImage (it moves the file to `~/Applications` and adds a hash to the name) and link the moved
If `yamt` is then not found, `~/.local/bin` is not on your PATH: add
`export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"` to your shell's start-up file (`~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`).
- **Arch Linux**: the AppImage, or build from source (below).
- **macOS**: the `.dmg`; drag yamt to Applications. The build is not signed, so macOS refuses to open it
("damaged", or "could not verify … free of malware") until you clear the download mark from the whole app.
Do this after every install or update:
- **Windows 10/11**: the `_x64-setup.exe`; it installs for your user only, without admin rights.
The build is not signed, so SmartScreen may warn: More info → Run anyway. yamt needs
[Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win) (`git.exe` on your PATH). The installer does
not put `yamt` on your PATH: add the folder its setup page installed to (under Windows'
Environment Variables, user `Path`), then open a new terminal. yamt is a console program: run it
from a terminal in the repository; started from the Start menu a console window opens beside it.

sections.title: Use
body: yamt                         # in the repository, when git stops with conflicts
yamt --diff                  # anywhere: compare any two texts side by side
yamt --diff=main...feature   # in a repository: review the changes between two commits
yamt --diff=main...feature --ai   # the same, with an AI to ask about each comment

`yamt --diff` opens a two-column compare instead of a merge: paste or type into both columns and the differences show as in the merge window. Format lays out JSON and XML (keys and values kept as written), the language drop-down picks the highlighting (Auto by default), and each comparison is a tab in the left panel. Tabs and their texts are kept between runs.

`yamt --diff=<a>...<b>` (or `<a>..<b>`, with git's meaning) reviews a commit range: the changed files on the left as GitLab lists them, and each file's two versions side by side, read-only. Hover a line number to start a comment thread there, as in GitLab. Each message can be queued with "Post", and "Send to GitLab (n)" sends the queue as pending comments of your merge request's review through `glab` (installed and logged in; it is enabled only while the merge request shows exactly this diff). Your own comments can be edited or deleted until they are sent. Threads are kept per repository and commit pair.

In a repository with a GitLab remote, both `--diff` windows have a merge-requests button left of the gear: the project's open merge requests, newest first. Each row shows the title, then `!12 · created … ago` and the size (`+120 −40 · 6 files`), with its open discussions, approvals, CI status (hover it for the failed jobs; a click opens a job's log in the browser) and GitLab's merge status as one icon (ready, has conflicts, needs rebase, blocked — the hover says why — or checking). A click on a row opens that merge request on GitLab in the browser. Filter by assignee, reviewer, label and draft with one click each; the filters are remembered per repository. A row's "Show Diff" button fetches that merge request's commits, without touching your branches or files, and opens its changes in a new window, lined up with the merge request for comments.

A row with conflicts has "Resolve conflicts of !12": in your own checkout (it refuses while you have uncommitted changes to tracked files, while git is busy with another operation, or when your local branch has commits GitLab's does not), yamt fetches the merge request's branch and its target, checks the branch out, merges the target into it without committing and opens the merge window. Commit merge then asks before pushing the branch to GitLab (never forced); Abort puts your checkout back as it was, branch included, even after a restart. While that merge is unfinished, its row offers "Continue merging" and the other rows wait. Merge requests from forks are not supported.

With `--ai`, each thread has "Ask AI": the AI (`omp acp` by default, set in Settings) answers in the thread, working in a temporary checkout of the right-hand commit. Its thinking and steps open under the answer, its edits show as diffs, and closing the window asks whether to keep its changes. A window started with `--ai` (`yamt --diff --ai` too) passes it on to the changes windows its merge-request page opens.

The gear opens the settings. Theme offers yamt's own Dark and Light and the default dark and light themes of WebStorm (Islands), VS Code (Dark/Light 2026), Zed (One) and Atom (One), in those editors' own colours: window, code and change colours, and their panel shapes.

sections.title: Language servers
body: yamt runs the language servers your project already has (it ships none): the result pane shows their problems as you type, and Ctrl+S formats with the project's formatter. It asks once per repository before starting them. It finds these by itself; settings add others:
- JavaScript and TypeScript: oxlint, oxfmt, Biome, TypeScript, eslint
- Rust: rust-analyzer · Go: gopls · C and C++: clangd
- PHP: Phpactor, PHPStan, Psalm, PHP-CS-Fixer, phpcs, Intelephense

sections.title: Make it feel built in
body: Even easier: let git open yamt by itself. Add this to `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`, and a plain `git merge`, `git pull`, `git rebase`, `git cherry-pick` or `git revert` that stops with conflicts opens the window; the command then ends with yamt's exit status.
It only acts in a terminal you type in: scripts, editors and piped output run git untouched.
`git mergetool` is not the way to start yamt: it runs the tool once per file, while yamt handles all files in one window.

sections.title: Build from source
body: You need the Rust toolchain from `rust-toolchain.toml` (installed by [rustup](https://rustup.rs) on the first `cargo` call), [pnpm](https://pnpm.io), and on Linux webkit2gtk-4.1 (Arch: `webkit2gtk-4.1`; Debian/Ubuntu: `libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev`).

sections.title: NVIDIA on Linux
sections.body: WebKitGTK's DMABUF renderer crashes on some NVIDIA setups. yamt switches it off by itself when the NVIDIA driver is loaded; a value you set for `WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER` wins.
